records.bodyText:
Kinlochleven Aluminium Smelter 
Photo of the remaining Power House and penstock pipelines running downhill from the Blackwater Dam (Known as the Conduit).
The Aluminium factory was built between 1905 and 1909, and this resulted the village of Kinlochleven that sprung up around it.
At its height there were 800 men employed there. The village became known as the Electric Village and had street lighting before Buckingham Palace!
The mountain in the background is Beinn Na Caillich. 
Built between 1905 and 1909 by the British Aluminium Company Ltd. Powered by the adjacent Kinlochleven hydroelectric scheme fed by the Blackwater Reservoir. 
At peak production the site employed up to 800 workers and produced around 200 tonnes of aluminium weekly at its peak.
Closure came in June 2000 under Alcan as the world's oldest and smallest operating smelter at the time.
The main smelter and carbon factory buildings were mostly demolished, though the original powerhouse remains in situ. Part of the site was converted into the "Aluminium Story" exhibition at the Kinlochleven Visitor Centre and Library and the Ice Factor climbing center. Power generated by the hydro scheme is now supplied to the Lochaber Aluminium Smelter in Fort William and the national grid.
The Lochaber Smelter in Fort William, Scotland, is the last operating primary aluminium smelter in the United Kingdom,
having opened in 1929.
Operated by ALVANCE British Aluminium, part of the GFG Alliance acquired in 2016.
Production capacity is around 45,000 to 48,000 tonnes of aluminium per year, employing just over 200 workers.
Powered by the adjacent Lochaber hydroelectric scheme via underground water tunnels and Francis turbines, giving it a low carbon footprint compared to global averages.
The process integrates industrial production with JAHAMA Highland Estates, managing roughly 114,000 acres of surrounding terrain.— in Kinlochleven.

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
WHAT happens when the government takes your land before it has even approved the project?
Grant Piper's family has run cattle at Uarbry, near Coolah in central New South Wales, since the 1840s.
In May 2023 a letter arrived from EnergyCo, the NSW Government's energy agency. NOTICE OF PROPOSED ACQUISITION. It said steel towers 65 metres high would go on a strip 70 metres wide, straight across the farm Grant grew up on. 110 farming families got the same letter.
In May 2024 the State Government took his land. A month later the Minns Labor government approved the project. Around him, developers plan more than 1,000 turbines and nine million solar panels, and the people of New South Wales pay for it.
"It's like having to pay the carpenter to build your own gallows." Grant Piper
Grant took his fight from Coolah to Canberra, where he opened the National Rally Against Reckless Renewables.
His district was the first Renewable Energy Zone in New South Wales. The state has declared four more. If you own land, your place could be next.
The book, “To Save a Beach: The Story of Reckless Renewables” tells Grant's story, and the stories of farmers and families fighting the rollout across Australia. 
Copies ordered before Christmas come with a limited edition Steven Nowakowski wildlife bookmark.
Order at sandrabourke.com, Connor Court Publishing or Amazon.
A percentage of profits will support the Australian Biodiversity Alliance (formerly Rainforest Reserves Australia).
#ToSaveABeach #RecklessRenewables #Coolah #NotCleanNotGreenNotZero

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
The first photo shows the Loch Quoich Reservoir and the Glen Quoich Bridge built around 1955. The dam is the largest rockfill dam in Scotland.
Very low water levels have exposed what is probably an unrecorded navvies camp close to the bridge, with rows of wooden posts, concrete foundations, foul drains and a brick cess tank.
Scattered finds include dated vulcanite beer bottle tops which support the mid 1950s date. This site won't often be above water.
Quoich Hydro Power Station (Commissioned 1955) Installed Capacity 22MW, located Highland region in the parish of Kilmonivaig. The power stations receives water from Loch Quoich via a tunnel with an integrated surge shaft located to the north of the station. The station contains a single 22MW undershot turbine which is deeply recessed to maximise the available head from the dam.
Water from the tailrace feeds into Loch Garry which is regulated by the Garry Dam and is then used for a second time in Invergarry Power Station. Loch Quoich Power Station is a good example of a medium sized power Station, housing a single large turbine and generator. The exterior design of the station echoes that of Invergarry with a recessed deep attic course containing narrow vents. The large central vent also dominates the main façade along with the large vehicular access doorways. There is a transformer subjstation to the east of the station behind a large coped boundary wall. 
Completed in 1955, it's a relatively small station with a single 22MW generator, and a gross head of 331ft. It's the only 'conventional' surface station in the Garrry/Moriston scheme; all the others are totally or partly underground. It's a very straightforward simple installation.
Quoich dam is a massive rockfill structure, 126ft high, 1050ft long, and 336ft wide at the base.
From the dam, water is led to the power station by a low-pressure tunnel, 12843ft long, and horseshoe in section, with an equivalent diameter of 11' 6". There are no sidestream intakes.
The low-pressure tunnel terminates at the base of the surge chamber, which is of the orifice type, with an upper expansion chamber. The chamber is 169ft deep, the top 40ft being 45ft in diameter (the expansion chamber), the remainder of the shaft being 30ft in diameter. From the base of the surge chamber, the water falls down a vertical high-pressure shaft, 158ft deep by 11' 6" in diameter.
From the base of the shaft, the remaining distance to the power station is covered by a high-pressure tunnel 1440ft long, followed by a steel penstock tunnel 820ft long, to the main inlet valve.
Inside the station, the machinery consists of a single vertical Francis turbine and generator unit. Somewhat unusually this is mounted horizontally, not vertically - this design was adopted to make erection easier. The alternator is rated at 22MW, which corresponds to approx. 30,000HP at the turbine. Tailrace is directly into the River Garry.
Because the construction of the Quoich dam stopped fish from getting into the upper reaches of the River Garry, a fish trap was built across the river just downstream from the power station. Here migrating salmon can be taken and stripped of their eggs, which are taken to a hatchery.
Quoich Dam is a good example of a large scale rockfill dam in Scotland, and is believed to be the largest in the country. The dam is faced in coursed random rubble, as are the gatehouse intake towers.
Quoich Dam lies the furthest west of all of the elements of the Great Glen Scheme. The dam provides the main storage capacity for the western section of the Great Glen scheme with water cascaded via Quoich Power Station into Loch Garry and Invergarry Power Station. The massive rockfill dam (the largest in Scotland) collects water from a large catchment which includes a number of smaller intakes from hill streams. The dam has a fixed spillway to the right hand side, utilising a natural channel in the rock. There is a spiral dispersal valve to the base of the dam and groundwater sluices. Water leaves the dam through the tunnel intake towers located on the upstream side of the dam to enter a tunnel which conveys it through to Quoich Power Station. The dam is faced in coursed random rubble, as are the gatehouse intake towers. This gives a good degree of architectural interest, with the rubble finish a relatively unusual feature in dam architecture under NoSHEB. The design is integrated across all of the features with a repeated balustrade feature which appears on the dam parapet and on both the intake towers and dispersal valvehouse.— at Loch Quoich.

This has been spoken about & raised at consultations,  but totally ignored by planners & developers !!
Microplastics and milk production… is an issue that hasn’t been discussed nearly enough 
Several proposed UK wind farms are proposed on farmland that supplies milk to some of our biggest producers. These are working farms where turbine blades, made from composite plastics, would shed fine micro- and nano-particles into the soil and waterways as they weather and erode.
What’s most concerning is that the PFAS and BPA-based coatings used in these blades are banned in many countries. Yet they’re still allowed to be imported and spread over prime agricultural land as the blades degrade.
These are the same pastures producing milk for families and international clients seeking powdered milk products.
This isn’t just about turbines in the wrong place, it’s about protecting our food chain, our farmland, and public health.
We’re calling on DEFRA, FSA, ASCA, Dairy UK, AHDB, NFU and regional governments to properly address this risk…
These questions are not even being asked of developers in planning!
• Disclosure of the proposed blade materials and coatings, including whether they contain PFAS or BPA-based resins.
• Independent assessment of erosion, particle dispersal and potential chemical release.
• Baseline testing and a monitoring programme appropriate to any identified risks.
• Public reporting and clear responsibility for preventing and addressing contamination.
#savethisland #rethinkrenewables #UKFarming #toxic #pollution

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Scotland exported 21.7 TWh of electricity and imported 0.9 TWh in 2025, resulting in net electricity exports of 20.8 TWh.
Key highlights for 2025:
Gross Exports: 21.7 TWh
Gross Imports: 0.9 TWh
Net Exports: 20.8 TWh (up from 19.7 TWh in 2024)
Indicative Wholesale Value: Approximately £1.7 B billion based on average wholesale day-ahead contract prices.
Renewable Generation: A record 38.5 TWh of renewable electricity was generated in Scotland in 2025.
Renewable Capacity: Reached 17.9 GW by the end of 2025.
Generation vs. Consumption: Scotland generated close to twice the electricity it consumed domestically, meeting roughly 113% of its annual electricity consumption through renewables. Most surplus power flows south to England via the GB transmission grid.
Over 10 TWh of renewable electricity was curtailed (switched off) in Scotland during 2025 due to transmission constraints. 
Scotland has 0.74 GW of operational pumped storage hydro (PSH) capacity.
Overall Hydro Generation: Total hydro generation across Scotland reached 4.6 TWh in 2025 as part of the broader renewable mix.
Major Existing Schemes: Operational pumped storage facilities include sites like Cruachan (Ben Cruachan) and Foyers on Loch Ness.
In 2025, the Torness nuclear power station generated 8.6 TWh approx.955517 % of total generation in Scotland and is due to close in 2030.
Eastern Green Links 1&2 are due to be commissioned in 2030s and will add 4 GW of additional export capacity. 
Inchcape Off shore Windfarm is due to add 1.1GW of new capacity in 2027.

EXCLUSIVE: Outlander star Sam Heughan reveals why he is 'against AI' and data centres
"I was told recently that Dumfries and Galloway, which is my home region, is going to have the biggest data centre. And I asked local politicians again, is this really what we want to be known for? And they told me, no, it's fine. And that the locals are happy. And I thought, well, the locals probably don't know about it, and the ones that do are probably not happy.
"There have been over 15 community groups that have come together. The campaigners in the Lammermuirs are so eloquent - and they've never done this before. They've never stood up and protested or had a voice. And I think it's unfair to put the pressure on local communities to do to do this.
“I think the people of Scotland don't want these data centres. The landowners do and the developers do, but the local communities, when they find out, and a lot of them don't find out till very late. I didn't find out about mine here at Bishopbriggs till quite late. And actually, there has been very little press about it here.
"It feels underhand, and it feels like the local communities don't want them.”

records.bodyText:
Shouldn’t we have a say where and how too?
Keep Fighting! It’s Working! Nearly Half Of The Data Centers Planned For 2026 Have Now Been Delayed Or Canceled
Communities across the U.S. are pushing back as large data centers continue expanding into local areas. These facilities require enormous amounts of electricity, and many also depend on substantial water resources for cooling.
An estimate from Sightline Climate suggests that 30% to 50% of large U.S. data center projects planned for completion in 2026 could face delays or cancellations. Power shortages, equipment delays and infrastructure constraints are among the factors contributing to these setbacks.
Community opposition can also influence whether projects move forward, although not every delay or cancellation is directly caused by local residents. The growing debate is forcing communities, utilities and developers to examine how AI infrastructure affects electricity, water, land and local resources.
As AI expansion continues, public participation is becoming an increasingly important part of decisions about where and how new data centers are built.
#fblifestyle #DataCenters #AI #Technology
